# Broadcast: broadcast-20261010-222734

**Prompt:** You are a player-experience researcher: cognitive psychology applied to games (agency, attribution, identity, motivation). Do a thorough ONLINE RESEARCH (search the web, cite real sources — academic papers, psychology-of-games research, GDC talks, player studies) on the topic below, then synthesize findings.

CONTEXT
Single-player idle/management RPG, D&D flavor. Party-based text quests on node graphs; checks roll on stats; real stakes (wound/death); exact numbers in preview. A core gimmick (e.g., infiltration-alarm) may admit ALTERNATIVE CHECK CHANNELS — DEX sneak, INT invisibility, CHA disguise — for the checks that move the core variable. Our emotional targets include attachment/sacrifice and "fair surprise"; the Director wants choices players can explain afterwards ("I lost X because of choice Y").

RESEARCH TOPIC — PLAYER PSYCHOLOGY OF ALTERNATIVE SOLUTION CHANNELS

1. EXPRESSIVE vs INSTRUMENTAL CHOICE: when is picking a channel an expression of identity ("I am a wizard, of course I cast invisibility") vs a cold optimization? Does expressive choice need mechanical differentiation to feel real, or does fiction differentiation suffice? Evidence on role-play identification (playing your build as a fantasy).
2. PARTY IDENTITY: does having a capability no alternative could provide create stronger attachment to specific party members? (The mage who carried the infiltration.) Links to endowment effect, attachment to named characters, "my party did it differently" as replay motivation.
3. THE DARK SIDE — when alternatives hurt: choice overload/paralysis (Iyengar, Schwartz on too many options); FOMO on locked channels ("the quest would have been easier with a rogue"); decision fatigue across many checks; regret when the chosen channel fails where another would have succeeded — does attribution ("my fault for choosing stealth") make failure MORE acceptable or LESS?
4. ATTRIBUTION & FAIRNESS: how do alternative channels interact with perceived fairness of failure? If the game shows the channel you couldn't take, does that feel like fairness (the world has depth) or taunting (look what you lack)?
5. PERCEIVED VARIETY vs ACTUAL VARIETY: does offering different channels on the same check increase perceived quest variety/replayability more than different checks would? Evidence on when "same problem different solution" feels like real content vs padding.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- 5-8 PRINCIPLES with evidence tags [academic research / shipped game / consensus / opinion].
- A "design implications" section: concrete dos/don'ts for our context (party of 1-4, exact previews, real stakes, attachment goals).
- Dense bullets; flag disagreements and replication-uncertain findings.

# Broadcast: broadcast-20261010-223444

**Prompt:** You are a senior narrative designer, expert in systemic narrative and text generation pipelines for games. Do a thorough ONLINE RESEARCH (search the web, cite real sources — narrative design talks, Failbetter/Emily Short essays, procgen-narrative postmortems) on the topic below, then synthesize findings.

CONTEXT
Single-player idle/management RPG, D&D flavor. Quests = node-graph text expeditions; check nodes carry title/body/verdict-flavor text (authored + LLM-assisted pipeline: brief → generate → validate → critique). A core gimmick (e.g., infiltration-alarm) may admit ALTERNATIVE CHECK CHANNELS — the SAME check node could be rolled as DEX (sneak), INT (invisibility spell) or CHA (disguise) depending on party/choice. Text must remain coherent with HOW the check was attempted.

RESEARCH TOPIC — NARRATIVE IMPLICATIONS OF ALTERNATIVE CHANNELS

1. SAME NODE, DIFFERENT FICTION: if one check can be attempted three ways, how do games handle the text? Options: (a) per-channel variants of setup + verdict flavor (3× text cost); (b) channel-agnostic setup + channel-specific outcome line; (c) parameterized template with channel tokens; (d) separate nodes per channel that rejoin (graph cost instead of text cost). Precedents: Failbetter storylets, conditional text in cRPGs, TTRPG module boxed-text conventions.
2. COHERENCE CONSTRAINTS PER CHANNEL: what the fiction must respect — magic has tells/costs (concentration, components, dispel wards), disguise implies social contact, stealth implies nobody saw you. How to encode per-channel "world rules" so generated text stays physically coherent (our domain-kit system already validates admissible entities/props/physics per biome — channels are a parallel axis).
3. FAILURE FICTION PER CHANNEL: failing invisibility ≠ failing stealth (spotted vs spell breaking vs cover blown). How much divergence is needed before players feel the fiction "saw" their choice?
4. AUTHORING COST CONTROL: combinatorial explosion of per-channel text — precedents for bounding it: write once + channel-conditional fragments; verdict-flavor per channel only on CRUCIAL beats; channel as modifier word/phrase vs full rewrite. Our rule: only checks that move the core variable get channels — does that bound it enough?
5. READER-PERCEPTION EVIDENCE: when do players notice/care that text acknowledged their approach? Minimal viable acknowledgment (one line? a word?) vs full scene variants.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- 5-8 PRINCIPLES with evidence tags [shipped game / research / consensus / opinion].
- A concrete text-architecture proposal for our pipeline (brief fields needed per channel: mustConvey/mayInvent additions).
- Cost-tier table: cheap acknowledgment → expensive variant, what to spend where.
- Dense bullets; flag disagreements.

title: prompt-t1-opportunity-graph
firstLines:
> **ERRATA (2026-10-11):** il contesto sotto descrive il gioco come "idle/management RPG" — errato. Il gioco e' un gestionale a tempo continuo SENZA progressione offline (posizionamento "second monitor"; decisione registrata in `marketing/steam/claim-ledger.md`). Le risposte AI che assumono idle/offline vanno lette con questa correzione.

You are a senior game systems designer at a AAA studio, expert in RPG mechanics, procedural generation and tabletop design. Do a thorough ONLINE RESEARCH (search the web, cite real sources — articles, GDC talks, papers, postmortems, dev blogs, TTRPG design essays) on the topic below, then synthesize findings.

CONTEXT
We are designing the quest system of a single-player idle/management RPG with D&D flavor. Structure: a village you manage (resources, buildings, roster of heroes+villagers) + expeditions = multi-phase text quests on a node graph (travel → approach choice → checks → objective → return). Each check node declares stats it rolls on (str/agi/end/int/perc/cha). Outcomes are gradient verdicts (epic fail/fail/almost/win/big win) + per-member wound/death risk. A quest has a CORE GIMMICK (central strategic problem, e.g. infiltration: an alarm escalating in named states quiet/alert/awake).

ABOVE the single quest we are designing the OPPORTUNITY LAYER: a meta-system deciding which quests appear, what unlocks them, what they open, and what they compete with.

DESIGN PROPOSAL UNDER EVALUATION (not yet decided): quests are nodes of an OPPORTUNITY GRAPH — not a linear tree "complete A → unlock B", but a graph where multiple paths can converge on the same opportunity and one quest can open several different doors. The graph represents persistent UNLOCK RELATIONS (a reward "access: contact X" opens node Y weeks later), not just temporal succession. We need a data model for: node types (quest offers, capabilities, accesses, information), edge types (unlocks/informs/prepares/discounts), persistence of opened edges in the save, and how the offer generator traverses the graph.

RESEARCH TOPIC — QUEST WEBS AND OPPORTUNITY GRAPHS
How do shipped games and published TTRPG techniques model non-linear quest/mission/opportunity structures?

Cover explicitly:
1. VIDEO GAME precedents for convergent/divergent quest structure: open-world RPGs with multiple entry paths to the same quest (Fallout NV quest flags, Skyrim radients vs hand-authored webs, The Witcher 3), nemesis-system style emergent relations (Shadow of Mordor), strategy-layer mission webs (XCOM, Battle Brothers contract board + ambitions, Pathfinder Kingmaker event cards), roguelike map-graph choice (Slay the Spire — you see the graph and choose the route; FTL sectors). What actually creates the feeling "the world offers me paths, not a queue"?
2. TTRPG precedents for unlock structure: Justin Alexander's NODE-BASED SCENARIO DESIGN (nodes = locations/NPCs/events, edges = clues/accesses — "three clue rule"), Apocalypse World FRONTS and Blades in the Dark FACTION CLOCKS (threats that advance on their own and create opportunities), "reactive dungeon" / hook-and-line sandbox structure. How do these represent "consequence opens a door"?
3. DATA MODELS: how is such a graph typically stored? Flag/variable systems (quest flags, world states), tag/key systems (Fallen London qualities = items+stats+story keys in one), prerequisite-expression systems (any-of/all-of requirement DSLs). Pros/cons of each for a small team.
4. PERSISTENCE & SCALE: what state must survive a run vs reset between runs? How do shipped games avoid graph state explosion or dead branches (missed nodes that never close)?
5. FAILURE PATTERNS: when do quest webs become unreadable (player can't tell what opened what), when does convergence make effort feel pointless, when does graph gating become artificial padding ("collect 3 keys")?

OUTPUT FORMAT
- 4-8 PRINCIPLES, each as an actionable rule ("do X because Y") with source/evidence attached. Tag each: [validated by shipped game] / [design theory] / [community consensus] / [opinion].
- A comparison table: precedent → node/edge model → what persists → how the player reads it.
- A short "If you only do 3 things" section — highest leverage for a small indie team.

firstLines:

You are a senior game systems designer at a AAA studio, expert in RPG mechanics, encounter design and procedural generation. Do a thorough ONLINE RESEARCH (search the web, cite real sources — articles, GDC talks, papers, postmortems, dev blogs, TTRPG design essays) on the topic below, then synthesize findings.

CONTEXT
We are designing the quest system of a single-player idle/management RPG with D&D flavor. Structure: a village you manage + expeditions = multi-phase text quests on a node graph. A quest has a CORE GIMMICK (central strategic problem: a race/progress variable, an alarm in named states, a flood, etc.), SCENE ARCHETYPES (reusable decision situations: acquire-something-at-a-cost, choose-who-exposes, ambiguous-information, incompatible-approaches, ordering-of-operations), and TWISTS (state-altering branches armed at run start). A DOMAIN KIT constrains the fiction (creatures, places, roles, physics). Generated quests must be validated automatically (reachability, non-cosmetic choices, difficulty band measured on a reference party).

DESIGN PROPOSAL UNDER EVALUATION (not yet decided): quests belong to macro FAMILIES (stealth/infiltration, combat/survival, exploration/discovery, diplomacy/interaction, preparation/resources). A family is NOT a single solution: it is a shared set of mechanics + a catalog of COMPATIBLE SOLUTIONS (skills, stats, items, preparations that let you approach it differently). Two levels: FAMILY MECHANIC (what makes the type recognizable — e.g. infiltration has an alarm variable, surveillance, noise) vs COMPATIBLE SOLUTIONS (DEX native, CHA via disguise, INT via invisibility). The same family mechanic should be reusable across many quests with different settings and stakes.

RESEARCH TOPIC — MISSION FAMILIES AND MECHANIC KITS
How do shipped games organize missions/encounters/levels into mechanic families that stay recognizable while varying content?

Cover explicitly:
1. VIDEO GAME precedents: XCOM/XCOM2 mission types (each type = distinct objective+timer shape but same tactical rules), Slay the Spire node types (combat/elite/event/rest/shop — instantly readable families), Into the Breach map objectives, Battle Brothers contract types, heist games (Payday mission categories), Hitman level = sandbox + opportunity system ("Mission Stories" as authored paths through the same space), MMO dungeon/role archetypes (tank/heal/dps pulls). What makes a mission type a "family" vs just a reskin?
2. ROGUELIKE/LIVEOPS modularity: how games define ROOM/ENCOUNTER ARCHETYPES that compose (Hades chamber types, Isaac room pools, Darkest Dungeon mission templates: kill/fetch/explore/escort with % explore goals). How do they keep families distinct without exploding authored content?
3. TTRPG precedents: encounter roles and "monster functions" (D&D 4e roles: soldier/lurker/controller — one family, many skins), Blades score types (score = assault/deception/stealth/social/transport/occult — a family taxonomy!), OSR "dungeon verbs", Justin Alexander's scenario structure types. What does a published taxonomy look like, and where does it break?
4. COMPATIBILITY CONTRACTS: how do systems declare which solutions/preparations are valid for a family without hand-authoring every pair? Skill-tag matching, resource typing, "challenge rating + toolkit" approaches. Any formal approaches (capability matrices, gating vocabularies)?
5. FAILURE PATTERNS: family taxonomies that collapsed (every mission becomes "kill the thing"), families that are pure flavor, catalogs that grow until unbalanceable, mechanics that only fit one family so families become silos.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- 4-8 PRINCIPLES, each as an actionable rule ("do X because Y") with source/evidence. Tag each: [validated by shipped game] / [design theory] / [community consensus] / [opinion].
- A comparison table: precedent → how it defines the family → where solutions/alternatives live → reuse mechanism.
- A short "If you only do 3 things" section — highest leverage for a small indie team.
- Dense bullets over prose. Flag where sources disagree.

You are a senior game systems designer at a AAA studio, expert in RPG mechanics and difficulty/progression design. Do a thorough ONLINE RESEARCH (search the web, cite real sources — articles, GDC talks, papers, postmortems, dev blogs, TTRPG design essays) on the topic below, then synthesize findings.

CONTEXT
We are designing the quest system of a single-player idle/management RPG with D&D flavor. A village you manage produces expeditions: multi-phase text quests on a node graph, resolved by party skill checks with real wound/death stakes (XCOM-like lethality). Quests arrive as OFFERS on a board — you can decline; declined/expired quests have consequences but are not punishments.

DESIGN PROPOSAL UNDER EVALUATION (not yet decided): quest REQUIREMENTS should not be only "min level" / "STR ≥ 10". Proposed taxonomy:
- ABSOLUTE ACCESS — without the condition the quest is unavailable; reserved for true impossibilities only.
- CAPABILITY — you can attempt it, but adequate skills produce good outcomes.
- COST-OR-RISK — you can attempt underprepared, accepting worse consequences (alarm, wounds, wasted time, compromised loot).
- OPTIMIZATION — a preparation that makes the quest more efficient/profitable.
Corollary: if missing equipment can be built/rented/won via another quest or token, the requirement is not absolute — it's a node in the opportunity graph. Underprepared departure = 3 cases: impossible / compensable at cost / attemptable at risk.

RESEARCH TOPIC — HARD GATES VS SOFT GATES: REQUIREMENT DESIGN
How do shipped games and TTRPGs implement access requirements without softlocking or railroading the player?

Cover explicitly:
1. HARD GATES: metroidvania ability gates (the canonical "you cannot pass without X"), Zelda-style item gates, level gates in MMOs/open worlds. When are hard gates good (orientation, pacing) vs bad (softlock anxiety, checklist feel)? How do shipped games telegraph "you are not ready — come back with X" honestly?
2. SOFT GATES: stat/skill thresholds that change outcomes not access (F:NV skill checks, Disco Elysium white/red checks — red checks reopen once!), difficulty-rating displays that let the player knowingly overreach (Darkest Dungeon: you CAN send level-1 heroes into a level-3 dungeon — the price is stress/casualties; Battle Brothers contract skulls; Souls-games: everything is "attemptable"), resource-bypass gates (pay/solve differently: Outer Worlds "pay, kill, or hack" pattern; immersive sim "many ways in").
3. EQUIPMENT-AS-KEY precedents: quests requiring a rope/boat/torch — how games avoid making fetch-of-item feel like padding (BOTW durability-as-cost, survival crafting prep lists, TTRPG "expedition supply" systems e.g. Torchbearer, OSR encumbrance-as-prep).
4. TELEGRAPHING UNDEPREPARED RISK: how games communicate "attemptable but dangerous" — danger bands, skull ratings, scout reports, "recommended party" UI. What makes the warning credible vs ignorable?
5. FAILURE PATTERNS: gates that are really padding (collect-N-keys), soft gates that deceive (fake choice: "you can attempt" = mathematically impossible), requirements that punish experimentation, level-scaling that erases the meaning of requirements.

OUTPUT FORMAT

You are a senior game systems designer at a AAA studio, expert in RPG mechanics and progression/reward design. Do a thorough ONLINE RESEARCH (search the web, cite real sources — articles, GDC talks, papers, postmortems, dev blogs, TTRPG design essays) on the topic below, then synthesize findings.

CONTEXT
We are designing the quest system of a single-player idle/management RPG with D&D flavor. Quests are nodes in an OPPORTUNITY GRAPH; party members have stats and (planned) equippable skills/spells/items. We want rewards and capabilities that change what is POSSIBLE, not just what is likely.

DESIGN PROPOSAL UNDER EVALUATION (not yet decided): rewards come in 8 categories — ACCESS (unlock places/contacts/quests), INFORMATION (reveal requirements/dangers/approaches), MITIGATION (reduce damage/risk/consequences), EXCEPTION (ignore a rule in a compatible situation), CONVERSION (turn a resource/capability into a different advantage), SYNERGY (boost capabilities already owned), PERMANENT INVESTMENT (change a possibility/rule for future quests), CONSUMABLE/COUNTERMEASURE (one-shot answer to a specific threat). Skills/spells/items can likewise OPEN an approach, NEGATE a consequence, TRANSFORM a check into a compatible one, REVEAL hidden info, BYPASS a requirement, or MODIFY a mechanic's operation (e.g. alarm accumulates slower). Key constraint: avoid an explosion of hand-authored per-quest exceptions — effects should attach to declared surfaces (core variables, requirement types, effect categories), not to individual cases.

RESEARCH TOPIC — REWARDS THAT OPEN DOORS; CAPABILITIES THAT CHANGE RULES
How do shipped games and TTRPGs implement rewards and abilities that alter possibility space rather than power level?

Cover explicitly:
1. UNLOCK-TYPE rewards: metroidvania abilities-as-keys (double jump = access), XCOM strategy layer rewards (research/projects unlocking strategic options not stat +X%), roguelike meta-progression (new cards/relics/characters unlocked, not stat boosts), faction/contact unlocks (Fallen London qualities, Hades keepsakes/npcs, Sunless Skies officers). Why do unlock rewards feel richer than +X rewards, and what do designers say about "verbs vs numbers"?
2. RULE-CHANGING capabilities: exception-based design in TCGs (MtG "cards may break rules — card text beats rulebook"; Yu-Gi-Oh keyword soups), roguelike relics/items that rewrite mechanics (Slay the Spire relics: Snecko Eye, Frozen Egg; Isaac items), TTRPG moves/feats that create exceptions (Dungeon World moves, 13th Age icon relationships, GUMSHOE investigative abilities — auto-success on core clues!), perks that change systems not numbers (F:NV perks, Outer Worlds flaws).
3. INFORMATION-AS-REWARD: games where intel/maps/scouting is the loot (submarine/scouting mechanics, Metroid prime scan visor debates, XCOM intel resource, Battle Brothers contracts revealing difficulty, TTRPG clue economies — Gumshoe "spend pool for extra info"). When is info a satisfying reward vs a non-reward?
4. ARCHITECTURE for rule-changing effects without exception-hell: how engines implement declarative effect surfaces (modifier systems, event/hook architectures, tagging capabilities) — e.g. how MtG-like games categorize continuous/replacement/triggered effects; how RPG systems stack "conditional modifiers" (Pathfinder bonus types debates!). Any precedents for a SMALL taxonomy of effect categories staying manageably small?
5. FAILURE PATTERNS: unlock rewards that became chores (keys-as-padding), exception effects that broke balance forever (MtG power-creep cards, Pathfinder bonus stacking), information rewards players felt cheated by, permanent investments that trivialized later content.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- 4-8 PRINCIPLES, each as an actionable rule with source/evidence. Tag each: [validated by shipped game] / [design theory] / [community consensus] / [opinion].
- A comparison table: precedent → what the capability/reward changes → declared surface vs hand-authored exception → balance control.
- A short "If you only do 3 things" section — highest leverage for a small indie team.
- Dense bullets over prose. Flag where sources disagree.

You are a senior game systems designer at a AAA studio, expert in RPG mechanics, procedural generation and information design. Do a thorough ONLINE RESEARCH (search the web, cite real sources — articles, GDC talks, papers, postmortems, dev blogs, TTRPG design essays) on the topic below, then synthesize findings.

CONTEXT
We are designing the quest system of a single-player idle/management RPG with D&D flavor. Quests arrive as procedural OFFERS on a board (~8-10/month vs 4-5 feasible — scarcity is the point). An EXPLORER role already reveals information about quests (secondary stats, dangers, surveillance — a canon rule). Quests belong to families (stealth/combat/exploration/diplomacy/preparation).

DESIGN PROPOSAL UNDER EVALUATION (not yet decided): two linked ideas.
(a) STEERABLE GENERATION — the player can bias the offer generator toward preferred families/tags; the preference influences the distribution WITHOUT guaranteeing it (control without removing uncertainty or competing opportunities).
(b) TRANSVERSAL INTEL RESOURCE — a single limited currency tied to operational information/prep (knowing a mission better is a spendable advantage), instead of per-family currencies (stealth-coins, diplomacy-coins...). Open question: how to keep it scarce and meaningful without making resources too interchangeable.

RESEARCH TOPIC — PLAYER-STEERED GENERATION AND INTEL AS A RESOURCE
How do shipped games let players influence procedurally generated content streams, and how is information made into a spendable resource?

Cover explicitly:
1. STEERING precedents: Slay the Spire map — you SEE the node graph and choose the route (visibility = steering without guarantee); FTL sector choice; Battle Brothers contract board + settlement specializations (different towns offer different contracts — geography as steering); XCOM2 choosing which missions to respond to (interception decisions); Invisible Inc campaign map (choose which facility to raid → chosen reward type); Wildfrost/roguelike drafting (class tags weighting card pools); Monster Train path forks. What is the mechanism — route choice, tag weighting, reroll currency, board curation?
2. DRAFT/WEIGHTING systems: how card-battle/roguelike systems weight offers (tag-weighted reward pools, banish/reroll mechanics, "choose 1 of 3" curation, STS rare card pity systems); TTRPG random-tables-with-biases (weighted tables, advantage/disadvantage on tables). What keeps steering meaningful vs making generation effectively authored-by-player?
3. INTEL CURRENCIES: XCOM intel resource (spent on missions/crafting/dark-site reveals), recon/scouting spending (pre-mission intel in Shadow Tactics/Desperados? recon in XCOM LW), Sunless Sea favors/secrets, Fallen London item-economy, TTRPG "preparedness"/flashback spends (Blades flashback mechanic — retroactive prep as a spend!), GUMSHOE spend pools, Divinity OS2 persuasion-as-investment. Which intel economies stayed interesting vs became hoarded/ignored?
4. VISIBILITY LADDERS: partial-info structures (you know the family but not the twist; you see difficulty band but not exact odds — we already ship exact-odds preview once engaged), fog-of-war info design. How much should steering cost vs reveal?
5. FAILURE PATTERNS: steering that made generation bland (always-optimal filter), currencies that multiplied until meaningless, info players never bought, reroll systems that removed all uncertainty and broke the game.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- 4-8 PRINCIPLES, each as an actionable rule with source/evidence. Tag each: [validated by shipped game] / [design theory] / [community consensus] / [opinion].
- A comparison table: precedent → steering mechanism → what stays uncertain → cost of steering/intel.
- A short "If you only do 3 things" section — highest leverage for a small indie team.

firstLines:

You are a senior game systems designer at a AAA studio, expert in strategy/management games and time-pressure design. Do a thorough ONLINE RESEARCH (search the web, cite real sources — articles, GDC talks, papers, postmortems, dev blogs, TTRPG design essays) on the topic below, then synthesize findings.

CONTEXT
We are designing a single-player idle/management RPG. A village produces expeditions: multi-phase text quests (days-long, real-time accelerated). The player can't do everything: ~8-10 quest offers/month vs 4-5 feasible; a quest costs ~28 human-days of labor, wounds make members unavailable for X days, the expedition leader rules capacity (tired/wounded leader → no expeditions). Declined/expired quests have consequences but are not punishments.

DESIGN PROPOSAL UNDER EVALUATION (not yet decided): TIME = three distinct concepts — DURATION (how long an activity occupies), DEADLINE (by when it must be done), OPPORTUNITY WINDOW (an interval where an action is advantageous/possible without being a hard deadline). Quests COMPETE: preparing for one may mean abandoning another, delaying an investment, or losing a window. Village growth has 3 dimensions: VISIBILITY (how many opportunities you see/how much you know), CAPABILITY (which you can attempt — skills/prep), OPERATIONAL CAPACITY (how many in parallel — humans, leaders, buildings; possibly multiple parties). Growth must NOT make everything trivially easier — more expeditions also means more wear and management pressure.

RESEARCH TOPIC — TIME PRESSURE, OPPORTUNITY WINDOWS, AND PARALLEL CAPACITY
How do shipped strategy/management/idle games implement competing time pressures and bounded parallelism?

Cover explicitly:
1. DEADLINE precedents — the good and the infamous: XCOM2 mission timers (the controversy: hidden per-mission turn timers vs strategic Avatar countdown — community verdict on which pressure was fair), XCOM EU abduction missions (3 sites, choose 1, 2 panic — the canonical "competing opportunities" mechanic!), Battle Brothers contract deadlines + world crises (late-game war/invasion forcing prioritization), Frostpunk storm/arcs, Stardew/Sun Haven festival windows, Paradox ticking events. When does a deadline feel like strategy vs like harassment?
2. OPPORTUNITY WINDOWS (not deadlines): seasonal events, caravan schedules, "the pass is open while the snow holds" patterns, Rimworld incidents/opportunities, MMO timed events critiques. Distinction between "expires if ignored" vs "better if timed" — any shipped examples that do BOTH well?
3. PARALLEL CAPACITY: how games bound simultaneity — expedition/assignment slots (idle games: multiple parties out at once; Fallout Shelter dweller assignment; Assassin's Creed Odyssey mercenary board? AFK Journey/idle RPGs send-N-teams), roster-stamina/fatigue as the real limiter (Battle Brothers injuries+fatigue forcing B-teams, XCOM wounded soldiers forcing bench depth — THE precedent for operational capacity being a roster problem not a slot problem), leader/officer limits (Total War army-per-general cap, Crusader Kings council slots, Pokemon?). Where does "send multiple parties" break for small rosters?
4. GROWTH WITHOUT TRIVIALIZATION: escalation coupling (XCOM: as you grow, threats grow — panopticon pressure; Darkest Dungeon: roster churn is the balance; incremental games' prestige loops). What keeps more-parallel-quests from becoming pure acceleration?
5. FAILURE PATTERNS: timers added later that fans rejected (XCOM2 launch timers vs WotC fixes), busywork opportunity spam (notification fatigue, "chore map"), capacity limits that felt artificial ("why can't I send a second team?" complaints), parallel systems that made downtime dead time.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- 4-8 PRINCIPLES, each as an actionable rule with source/evidence. Tag each: [validated by shipped game] / [design theory] / [community consensus] / [opinion].
- A comparison table: precedent → time-pressure model → parallelism limiter → growth-pressure coupling.
- A short "If you only do 3 things" section — highest leverage for a small indie team.
- Dense bullets over prose. Flag where sources disagree.

firstLines:
> **ERRATA (2026-10-11):** il contesto sotto descrive il gioco come "idle/management RPG" — errato. Il gioco e' un gestionale a tempo continuo SENZA progressione offline (posizionamento "second monitor"; decisione registrata in `marketing/steam/claim-ledger.md`). Le risposte AI che assumono idle/offline vanno lette con questa correzione.

You are a senior game systems designer at a AAA studio, expert in prototyping methodology and simulation-driven design. Do a thorough ONLINE RESEARCH (search the web, cite real sources — articles, GDC talks, papers, postmortems, dev blogs, design methodology essays) on the topic below, then synthesize findings.

CONTEXT
We are designing a single-player idle/management RPG. We just finished a design layer ABOVE single quests: an OPPORTUNITY LAYER (quest families, requirement taxonomy, door-opening rewards, steerable offer generation, three kinds of time — duration/deadline/window — and village capacity in 3 dimensions: visibility/capability/operational-capacity). None of it is implemented yet; the single-quest engine exists (node-graph expeditions, skill checks, wound/death, Monte Carlo validation on authored scenario graphs).

DESIGN PROPOSAL UNDER EVALUATION (not yet decided): the first test of the meta-layer should be WITHOUT COMBAT — a minimal prototype validating the opportunity structure itself: (a) requirements correctly produce access/risk/efficiency differences; (b) multiple READABLE ways exist to satisfy the same requirement; (c) skills/rewards open genuinely different possibilities; (d) the explorer can be steered toward families; (e) quests generate future opportunities without a rigid sequence; (f) deadlines/concurrent activities produce real strategic decisions. Setup: 3 families × 3 difficulty tiers, existing stats, configurable requirements, FIXED configurable rewards (no direct stat increments — reward spirals out of scope for v0).

RESEARCH TOPIC — HOW TO PROTOTYPE A META-LAYER: METHODOLOGY
What are proven methods for validating a meta-game/economy/opportunity structure BEFORE building the full game?

Cover explicitly:
1. STRUCTURE-FIRST prototyping precedents: Soren Johnson / Cole Wehrle talks on prototyping the strategy layer; Sid Meier "one prototype" practices; how XCOM's strategy layer was paper-first (Jake Solomon talks?); spreadsheet/simulation-driven design (designing economy models in sheets before code — "machinations" framework by Joris Dormans, Machinations.io tool — formal economy diagrams you can simulate!). TTRPG solo-playtesting methods for meta-systems.
2. SIMULATION-BEFORE-UI: cases where Monte Carlo / agent-based sims validated meta-game structure (battle for balance — how auto-battler/idle devs validate pacing; AI-vs-AI self-play for board game balance — e.g. how Slay the Spire reportedly used metrics? what devs say about sim-driven balance); what CAN'T be validated in sim (fun, legibility) and needs humans.
3. READABILITY/LEGIBILITY testing of meta-systems: how to test "the player understands what opened what" — paper prototypes, Wizard-of-Oz text prototypes, single-page tabletop versions (digital game jam → boardgame conversions), tutorial-free comprehension tests. Any precedents from grand-strategy/4X tutorialization postmortems?
4. MINIMUM VIABLE META: how small can the first version be while still exposing real problems — "one loop" tests, fake-data harnesses, dev-console-driven playtests (play the system via commands, no UI). What metrics to pre-commit (decision distribution, dominant-strategy detection, dead-option rate, opportunity-miss rate)?
5. FAILURE PATTERNS: prototypes that validated nothing because scope crept; sims that produced false confidence (model != game); meta-layers that tested fine but collapsed on real UI; testing generation quality with too few samples.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- 4-8 PRINCIPLES, each as an actionable rule with source/evidence. Tag each: [validated by shipped game/method] / [design theory] / [community consensus] / [opinion].
- A comparison table: method → what it validates → what it can't validate → cost for a small team.
- A short "If you only do 3 things" section — highest leverage for a small indie team.

title: T1 — Grafo delle opportunità / quest webs: struttura dati e persistenza
firstLines:
# T1 — Grafo delle opportunità / quest webs: struttura dati e persistenza

**Status: RESEARCH SYNTHESIS (PROPOSAL)** — 2026-10-11
**Fonti:** broadcast multi-AI (chatgpt, gemini, deepseek successi; claude fallito su selettore, grok output vuoto) + ricerca web propria. Raw: `t1-opportunity-graph/BROADCAST.md`.
**File correlati:** `context/QUEST_OPPORTUNITY_LAYER.md` §2, `context/OPEN.md` OPEN-019.

---

## 1. La domanda e la risposta sintetica

Domanda: come strutturare e persistere un grafo dove nodi = opportunità e archi = "porta aperta" (requisito soddisfatto, capacità acquisita, informazione, accesso)?

Risposta trasversale delle fonti: **non costruire un grafo di quest — costruire un grafo di entità di mondo**. I nodi persistenti sono accessi, contatti, luoghi, favori e clocks; le quest sono *offerte transitorie* che attraversano quei nodi. Questo è esattamente il modello Fallen London (storylets + qualities) e la lettura di Battle Brothers offerta da deepseek.

## 2. Modello dati raccomandato: qualities + offer generator

Consenso forte (gemini + deepseek): per un team piccolo il modello corretto è **Fallen London puro**:

- **Stato salvato = dizionario piatto di qualities** (`{"access:thieves_guild": 1, "intel:cult_lair": 1, "clock:watch_alert": 4}`). Serializzazione, debug e ispezione triviali. Fallen London ha fatto emergere 60+ pattern narrativi da questa singola primitiva.
- **Offer generator** = query periodica: "quali candidati hanno tutti i `requires` soddisfatti dallo stato corrente?" → produce le offerte visibili. La quest istanziata nasce solo a quel punto (coerente con la regola chain-quest: "mai generare tutte le scene in anticipo").
- **Nessun DSL finché il grafo è sotto le centinaia di nodi.** Il JSON con `all_of`/`any_of` mostrato da gemini è già il massimo della complessità necessaria. Qualities possono esprimere quasi tutto.

**Due scope separati esplicitamente** (deepseek, punto 7 — il bug più comune nei save di RPG long-lived):
- `WorldState` — persiste tra spedizioni: fazioni, contatti, reputazione, clocks.
- `RunState` — per spedizione: ferite, posizione, risorse temporanee.

# T2 — Famiglie di quest come mechanic kits: definizione, soluzioni compatibili, riuso

**Status: RESEARCH SYNTHESIS (PROPOSAL)** — 2026-10-11
**Fonti:** broadcast multi-AI (gemini, deepseek, claude successi e sostanziosi; chatgpt caricamento fallito, grok vuoto) + ricerca web propria (XCOM EU/XCOM2, Darkest Dungeon). Raw: `t2-quest-families/BROADCAST.md`.
**File correlati:** `context/QUEST_OPPORTUNITY_LAYER.md` §3, `context/QUEST_GENERATION_ARCHITECTURE.md`.

---

## 1. Risposta sintetica

Consenso quasi totale delle tre AI utili: **una famiglia si definisce per la sua "signature pressure" — variabile di stato, come si muove, condizione di stop — non per la fiction né per il verbo dell'obiettivo**. Questo è esattamente il nostro "core gimmick" riletto a livello di tassonomia: la famiglia *è* una classe di gimmick.

- XCOM 2: "Rescue VIP" e "Kill the General" usano le stesse regole tattiche; differiscono nella variabile di pressione (security level che scala a 10 vs turn timer prima che il target fugga).
- Darkest Dungeon: 5 template (Cleanse 100% fight / Explore 90% stanze / Kill boss / Activate 3 altari / Gather 3 reliquie) — stesso dungeon, stesso combattimento, diversa condizione di stop.
- Blades in the Dark: 6 score type (Assault, Deception, Stealth, Social, Transport, Occult) — ognuno richiede un "detail" specifico e definisce la forma dell'engagement, non la soluzione.

## 2. Il "swap test" — criterio formale per famiglia vs reskin

Il contributo più utile di claude: **se scambi la fiction e la sequenza decisionale ottimale, le poste in gioco e il failure mode restano identici → è un reskin, non una famiglia**. Caso negativo: Battle Brothers, dove i contract types differiscono quasi solo in paga/difficoltà e ogni contratto finisce in combattimento.

Regola operativa: **una famiglia si merita di esistere solo se almeno una decisione ottimale in essa è subottimale altrove**. Verificabile nel nostro validatore su reference party — va aggiunto come check: due quest di famiglie diverse non possono avere strategia ottima identica.

Formulazione gemini equivalente: "riesci a descrivere la state machine della famiglia in una frase?" (*"Allarme 0→10; ogni detection +1; abort a 10"*). Se sì, è una famiglia; se la frase è uguale a un'altra, è un reskin.

## 3. Dove vivono le soluzioni: preparation layer + capability tags

title: T3 — Tassonomia requisiti e hard vs soft gates
firstLines:
# T3 — Tassonomia requisiti e hard vs soft gates

**Status: RESEARCH SYNTHESIS (PROPOSAL)** — 2026-10-11
**Fonti:** broadcast multi-AI (deepseek, gemini, claude successi sostanziosi; chatgpt echo prompt, grok vuoto) + ricerca propria (Disco Elysium, metroidvania gating, GUMSHOE). Raw: `t3-requirements/BROADCAST.md`.
**File correlati:** `context/QUEST_OPPORTUNITY_LAYER.md` §4, `context/OPEN.md` OPEN-020.

---

## 1. Risposta sintetica

La nostra tassonomia a 4 tipi (accesso assoluto / capacità / costo-o-rischio / ottimizzazione) **regge il confronto coi precedenti**. Le AI convergono sul raffinarla così: i gate non vanno pensati come "proprietà della quest" ma come **stati calcolati dell'offerta**, con telegraphing onesto e prezzi proporzionali al gap.

La distinzione più utile che emerge (deepseek): **hard gate = per insegnare, non per padding**. Un gate assoluto è giustificato solo se ha una ragione di pacing/orientamento O è una vera impossibilità logica — e il giocatore deve vedere la serratura e sapere dove sta la chiave.

## 2. Regole consolidate sui 4 tipi

### Accesso assoluto
- Riservato a impossibilità logiche/narrative vere (oceano senza nave, vuoto tossico senza respiratore).
- **Telegraphing: fallimento cospicuo, non testo.** Il muro si vede, il motivo si capisce in un tentativo, il costo dell'urto è zero. Anti-pattern: muro invisibile o gate che punisce il tentativo.
- **"Lock near the key"** (Mark Brown su Metroid Dread): meno serrature per chiave, chiave vicina alla serratura.
- C'è sempre un motivo di pacing/orientamento — se non c'è, non deve essere assoluto.

### Capacità (soft gate che cambia l'esito, non l'accesso)
- Modello F:NV / Outer Worlds: **mostra l'opzione bloccata e la sua linea di fallimento**. Il giocatore sa che esiste e che non è pronto. Sawyer: "l'opzione sbloccata può essere scelta, ma a volte non è una buona idea"; i check sui percorsi critici sono i più gratificanti.
- **White vs Red (Disco Elysium)**: white = riapribile dopo skill-up o nuova info; red = one-shot, conseguenza permanente — e il fallimento è narrativamente generativo, spesso più interessante del successo. *Correzione di claude al nostro brief: i red check NON si riaprono; se vogliamo un check riapribile-una-volta è design nostro.*

# T4 — Ricompense-porta e capacità che cambiano le regole

**Status: RESEARCH SYNTHESIS (PROPOSAL)** — 2026-10-11
**Fonti:** broadcast multi-AI (gemini + deepseek-via-retry sostanziosi; claude troncato/fallito, chatgpt/grok inutilizzabili) + ricerca propria (Rosewater "rules for rule breaking", GUMSHOE, Slay the Spire, Battle Brothers). Raw: `t4-rewards-capabilities/BROADCAST.md` + `t4-rewards-capabilities-retry/BROADCAST.md`.
**File correlati:** `context/QUEST_OPPORTUNITY_LAYER.md` §5, QUEST_RULES §7 (canali).

---

## 1. Risposta sintetica

Consenso tra gemini e la mia ricerca: **le ricompense che contano sono "verbi, non numeri"** — espandono lo spazio delle azioni possibili invece di rendere più efficiente un'azione esistente. E il modo ingegneristicamente corretto di implementarle non sono eccezioni per-quest, ma **un set chiuso di "superfici" dichiarate su cui le capacità si agganciano come interceptor**.

## 2. Verbi > numeri (lateral agency > vertical scaling)

- Le abilità metroidvania (double jump) sono *chiave e verbo insieme*: aprono geometria e cambiano il moveset (GMTK). XCOM EU separa upgrade numerici (armatura) da unlock strategici (Alien Containment → loop completamente nuovo: cattura vivi → interrogazioni → tech).
- F:NV: perk come *Terrifying Presence* creano opzioni di dialogo nuove che bypassano interi combattimenti — una capability = un verbo nuovo, non +10%.
- GUMSHOE (Laws): possedere l'Investigative Ability rende la raccolta della core clue **successo automatico senza tiro** — la capacità rimuove un intero sottosistema di rischio, è il caso estremo di "cambia le regole".
- **Regola di lateral agency**: i reward di alto livello espandono il grafo (nuovi nodi, check alternativi), non inflazionano i numeri — la stat inflation produce power creep e una sola strategia dominante. Meta-progressione roguelike corretta = unlock laterali (nuove classi, nuovi pool), non stat verticali.

## 3. L'architettura chiave: "Declared Surface" pattern

Il contributo più actionable di gemini, direttamente mappabile sul nostro sistema:

- **Il motore espone un set chiuso di superfici**: tipi di requisito (`HAS_TRAIT`, `REQUIRES_ITEM`, `STAT_CHECK`, `RISK`), hook di evento (`ON_CHECK_ROLL`, `ON_NODE_ENTER`, `ON_RESOURCE_DRAIN`).
- **Le capacità/reward si dichiarano come interceptor** su quelle superfici, con 5 operazioni:

title: T5 — Steering della generazione e intel come risorsa trasversale
firstLines:
# T5 — Steering della generazione e intel come risorsa trasversale

**Status: RESEARCH SYNTHESIS (PROPOSAL)** — 2026-10-11
**Fonti:** broadcast multi-AI (gemini unico sostanzioso; claude/deepseek falliti su selettore UI, chatgpt/grok inutilizzabili) + ricerca propria (L4D AI Director, WAWLT author goals, weighted pools, StS). Raw: `t5-steering-intel/BROADCAST.md`.
**File correlati:** `context/QUEST_OPPORTUNITY_LAYER.md` §6, `context/OPEN.md` OPEN-021.

---

## 1. Risposta sintetica

Il principio unificante (gemini): **lo steering del giocatore deve modellare le scelte, non dettare gli esiti**. Tradotto sul nostro caso: l'esploratore orientabile agisce sui *pesi* della distribuzione delle offerte, mai come filtro duro né garanzia; l'intel è una valuta trasversale che compra visibilità E mitigazione, con costo-opportunità tra famiglie.

La mia ricerca aggiunge due precedenti forti che la broadcast non ha citato:
- **L4D AI Director** (Booth, GDC 2009): "structured unpredictability" — layer di algoritmi semplici e ispezionabili che leggono lo stato del giocatore e modulano ciò che viene generato. Il nostro offer generator può adottare lo stesso principio: niente black box, pesi dichiarati e leggibili.
- **WAWLT "Author Goals"** (Kremins et al., FDG 2020): un linguaggio di intenti del giocatore ("coinvolgi personaggio X", "introduci falsa pista") che il generatore usa come funzione di scoring sulle azioni possibili — il precedente più vicino all'"orientamento dell'esploratore" come meccanica esplicita.

## 2. I 5 meccanismi di steering nei giochi shipped

| Meccanismo | Precedente | Cosa resta incerto | Lezione |
|---|---|---|---|
| Scelta di rotta spaziale | StS, FTL, Monster Train | Dettagli encounter/reward | La mappa visibile fa steering senza UI filtro |
| Curation geografica/fazioni | Battle Brothers, XCOM2, Invisible Inc. | Pericoli, twist, termini | Pesi famiglia legati a luoghi/fazioni → steering diegetico, non toggle menu |
| Pesi e bias sui pool | Wildfrost, TTRPG weighted tables | Rarità, slot non pesati | Equipaggiare un tag = moltiplicatore di peso (+150%) sul pool |
| Selezione curata "1 di N" | Hades, Monster Train | Il draft successivo | Attenzione ai reroll illimitati → board-fishing |
| Reroll a pagamento | — | — | Reroll gratis invalida la scarsità del board |

## 1. Risposta sintetica

Il precedente più forte **non è "più timer"** ma *far scegliere al giocatore quali impegni di valore onorare, con costi leggibili e recuperabili*. La nostra tripartizione durata/scadenza/finestra regge e va formalizzata come **contratto di design**: sono tre domande diverse — cosa resta occupato / cosa cambia se non agisco / cosa diventa più vantaggioso in un intervallo.

Consenso chatgpt+grok+mia ricerca:
- Deadline dure = eccezione, per fiction che le giustifica.
- Finestre ricorrenti/degradanti = il default per la pressione temporale.
- Concorrenza = vincoli operativi reali (persone, leader, recupero), **mai slot arbitrari**.
- Crescita = escalation del mondo, non accelerazione pura.

## 2. Deadline: strategia vs harassment

La tabella di fairness sintetizzata da chatgpt è il criterio operativo:

| Condizione | Deadline strategica | Harassment |
|---|---|---|
| Informazione | Cutoff e conseguenza noti | Timer oscuro |

title: T7 — Metodologia di prototipo per il meta-layer (senza combattimento)
firstLines:
# T7 — Metodologia di prototipo per il meta-layer (senza combattimento)

**Status: RESEARCH SYNTHESIS (PROPOSAL)** — 2026-10-11
**Fonti:** broadcast multi-AI (chatgpt ~1100 righe di altissima qualità, deepseek e gemini solidi; grok scarso) + ricerca propria (Machinations/Dormans, MCTS playtest QMUL, McDie, Sid Meier double-or-halve). Raw: `t7-prototype-meta/BROADCAST.md`.
**File correlati:** `context/QUEST_OPPORTUNITY_LAYER.md` §9 (perimetro test), `plans/PLAN-029-quest-gen-lab-operativa.md` (il Lab esiste già come harness).

---

## 1. Verdict

Il prototipo meta-layer senza combattimento è la scelta giusta — **a condizione che sia trattato come un decision system giocabile, non una miniatura del gioco finale**. Il loop deve essere completo (stato villaggio → generazione offerte → commitment → risoluzione → paesaggio opportunità cambiato → ripeti) ma senza le parti che non servono all'ipotesi: niente combat, ferite, UI village, prosa narrativa.

Consenso delle 3 AI utili: **tre metodi complementari in sequenza**, ognuno risponde a una domanda diversa —
1. **Struttura** (paper/spreadsheet/Machinations): le regole producono scelte reali?
2. **Simulazione** (harness deterministico + policy agents): esistono strategie dominanti/dead option/deadlock?
3. **Comprensione umana** (Wizard-of-Oz/playtest): il giocatore *capisce* cosa ha aperto cosa?

Un simulatore può provare che tre strategie hanno esiti diversi; non può provare che un umano le noti o le trovi interessanti.

## 2. La sequenza a 3 gate proposta (chatgpt)

### Gate A — Correttezza strutturale (automatico)
Regole deterministiche: requisiti, effetti reward, capacità, tempo, generazione offerte. Test delle 3 dimensioni di capacità e dei 3 tipi di tempo **separatamente e in combinazione**. Exit: nessuno stato impossibile, nessun bypass non intenzionale. *Se durata/scadenza/finestra collassano in un unico timestamp di scadenza, il tempo non è validato.*

### Gate B — Viabilità strategica (simulazione + self-play)

title: Broadcast: broadcast-20261011-210750
firstLines:
# Broadcast: broadcast-20261011-210750

**Prompt:** You are a senior game systems designer at a AAA studio, expert in RPG mechanics, procedural generation and tabletop design. Do a thorough ONLINE RESEARCH (search the web, cite real sources — articles, GDC talks, papers, postmortems, dev blogs, TTRPG design essays) on the topic below, then synthesize findings.

CONTEXT
We are designing the quest system of a single-player idle/management RPG with D&D flavor. Structure: a village you manage (resources, buildings, roster of heroes+villagers) + expeditions = multi-phase text quests on a node graph (travel → approach choice → checks → objective → return). Each check node declares stats it rolls on (str/agi/end/int/perc/cha). Outcomes are gradient verdicts (epic fail/fail/almost/win/big win) + per-member wound/death risk. A quest has a CORE GIMMICK (central strategic problem, e.g. infiltration: an alarm escalating in named states quiet/alert/awake).

ABOVE the single quest we are designing the OPPORTUNITY LAYER: a meta-system deciding which quests appear, what unlocks them, what they open, and what they compete with.

DESIGN PROPOSAL UNDER EVALUATION (not yet decided): quests are nodes of an OPPORTUNITY GRAPH — not a linear tree "complete A → unlock B", but a graph where multiple paths can converge on the same opportunity and one quest can open several different doors. The graph represents persistent UNLOCK RELATIONS (a reward "access: contact X" opens node Y weeks later), not just temporal succession. We need a data model for: node types (quest offers, capabilities, accesses, information), edge types (unlocks/informs/prepares/discounts), persistence of opened edges in the save, and how the offer generator traverses the graph.

RESEARCH TOPIC — QUEST WEBS AND OPPORTUNITY GRAPHS
How do shipped games and published TTRPG techniques model non-linear quest/mission/opportunity structures?

Cover explicitly:
1. VIDEO GAME precedents for convergent/divergent quest structure: open-world RPGs with multiple entry paths to the same quest (Fallout NV quest flags, Skyrim radients vs hand-authored webs, The Witcher 3), nemesis-system style emergent relations (Shadow of Mordor), strategy-layer mission webs (XCOM, Battle Brothers contract board + ambitions, Pathfinder Kingmaker event cards), roguelike map-graph choice (Slay the Spire — you see the graph and choose the route; FTL sectors). What actually creates the feeling "the world offers me paths, not a queue"?
2. TTRPG precedents for unlock structure: Justin Alexander's NODE-BASED SCENARIO DESIGN (nodes = locations/NPCs/events, edges = clues/accesses — "three clue rule"), Apocalypse World FRONTS and Blades in the Dark FACTION CLOCKS (threats that advance on their own and create opportunities), "reactive dungeon" / hook-and-line sandbox structure. How do these represent "consequence opens a door"?
3. DATA MODELS: how is such a graph typically stored? Flag/variable systems (quest flags, world states), tag/key systems (Fallen London qualities = items+stats+story keys in one), prerequisite-expression systems (any-of/all-of requirement DSLs). Pros/cons of each for a small team.
4. PERSISTENCE & SCALE: what state must survive a run vs reset between runs? How do shipped games avoid graph state explosion or dead branches (missed nodes that never close)?
5. FAILURE PATTERNS: when do quest webs become unreadable (player can't tell what opened what), when does convergence make effort feel pointless, when does graph gating become artificial padding ("collect 3 keys")?

OUTPUT FORMAT
- 4-8 PRINCIPLES, each as an actionable rule ("do X because Y") with source/evidence attached. Tag each: [validated by shipped game] / [design theory] / [community consensus] / [opinion].
- A comparison table: precedent → node/edge model → what persists → how the player reads it.
- A short "If you only do 3 things" section — highest leverage for a small indie team.

# Broadcast: broadcast-20261011-211037

**Prompt:** You are a senior game systems designer at a AAA studio, expert in RPG mechanics, encounter design and procedural generation. Do a thorough ONLINE RESEARCH (search the web, cite real sources — articles, GDC talks, papers, postmortems, dev blogs, TTRPG design essays) on the topic below, then synthesize findings.

CONTEXT
We are designing the quest system of a single-player idle/management RPG with D&D flavor. Structure: a village you manage + expeditions = multi-phase text quests on a node graph. A quest has a CORE GIMMICK (central strategic problem: a race/progress variable, an alarm in named states, a flood, etc.), SCENE ARCHETYPES (reusable decision situations: acquire-something-at-a-cost, choose-who-exposes, ambiguous-information, incompatible-approaches, ordering-of-operations), and TWISTS (state-altering branches armed at run start). A DOMAIN KIT constrains the fiction (creatures, places, roles, physics). Generated quests must be validated automatically (reachability, non-cosmetic choices, difficulty band measured on a reference party).

DESIGN PROPOSAL UNDER EVALUATION (not yet decided): quests belong to macro FAMILIES (stealth/infiltration, combat/survival, exploration/discovery, diplomacy/interaction, preparation/resources). A family is NOT a single solution: it is a shared set of mechanics + a catalog of COMPATIBLE SOLUTIONS (skills, stats, items, preparations that let you approach it differently). Two levels: FAMILY MECHANIC (what makes the type recognizable — e.g. infiltration has an alarm variable, surveillance, noise) vs COMPATIBLE SOLUTIONS (DEX native, CHA via disguise, INT via invisibility). The same family mechanic should be reusable across many quests with different settings and stakes.

RESEARCH TOPIC — MISSION FAMILIES AND MECHANIC KITS
How do shipped games organize missions/encounters/levels into mechanic families that stay recognizable while varying content?

Cover explicitly:
1. VIDEO GAME precedents: XCOM/XCOM2 mission types (each type = distinct objective+timer shape but same tactical rules), Slay the Spire node types (combat/elite/event/rest/shop — instantly readable families), Into the Breach map objectives, Battle Brothers contract types, heist games (Payday mission categories), Hitman level = sandbox + opportunity system ("Mission Stories" as authored paths through the same space), MMO dungeon/role archetypes (tank/heal/dps pulls). What makes a mission type a "family" vs just a reskin?
2. ROGUELIKE/LIVEOPS modularity: how games define ROOM/ENCOUNTER ARCHETYPES that compose (Hades chamber types, Isaac room pools, Darkest Dungeon mission templates: kill/fetch/explore/escort with % explore goals). How do they keep families distinct without exploding authored content?
3. TTRPG precedents: encounter roles and "monster functions" (D&D 4e roles: soldier/lurker/controller — one family, many skins), Blades score types (score = assault/deception/stealth/social/transport/occult — a family taxonomy!), OSR "dungeon verbs", Justin Alexander's scenario structure types. What does a published taxonomy look like, and where does it break?
4. COMPATIBILITY CONTRACTS: how do systems declare which solutions/preparations are valid for a family without hand-authoring every pair? Skill-tag matching, resource typing, "challenge rating + toolkit" approaches. Any formal approaches (capability matrices, gating vocabularies)?
5. FAILURE PATTERNS: family taxonomies that collapsed (every mission becomes "kill the thing"), families that are pure flavor, catalogs that grow until unbalanceable, mechanics that only fit one family so families become silos.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- 4-8 PRINCIPLES, each as an actionable rule ("do X because Y") with source/evidence. Tag each: [validated by shipped game] / [design theory] / [community consensus] / [opinion].
- A comparison table: precedent → how it defines the family → where solutions/alternatives live → reuse mechanism.
- A short "If you only do 3 things" section — highest leverage for a small indie team.
- Dense bullets over prose. Flag where sources disagree.

# Broadcast: broadcast-20261011-211453

**Prompt:** You are a senior game systems designer at a AAA studio, expert in RPG mechanics and difficulty/progression design. Do a thorough ONLINE RESEARCH (search the web, cite real sources — articles, GDC talks, papers, postmortems, dev blogs, TTRPG design essays) on the topic below, then synthesize findings.

CONTEXT
We are designing the quest system of a single-player idle/management RPG with D&D flavor. A village you manage produces expeditions: multi-phase text quests on a node graph, resolved by party skill checks with real wound/death stakes (XCOM-like lethality). Quests arrive as OFFERS on a board — you can decline; declined/expired quests have consequences but are not punishments.

DESIGN PROPOSAL UNDER EVALUATION (not yet decided): quest REQUIREMENTS should not be only "min level" / "STR ≥ 10". Proposed taxonomy:
- ABSOLUTE ACCESS — without the condition the quest is unavailable; reserved for true impossibilities only.
- CAPABILITY — you can attempt it, but adequate skills produce good outcomes.
- COST-OR-RISK — you can attempt underprepared, accepting worse consequences (alarm, wounds, wasted time, compromised loot).
- OPTIMIZATION — a preparation that makes the quest more efficient/profitable.
Corollary: if missing equipment can be built/rented/won via another quest or token, the requirement is not absolute — it's a node in the opportunity graph. Underprepared departure = 3 cases: impossible / compensable at cost / attemptable at risk.

RESEARCH TOPIC — HARD GATES VS SOFT GATES: REQUIREMENT DESIGN
How do shipped games and TTRPGs implement access requirements without softlocking or railroading the player?

Cover explicitly:
1. HARD GATES: metroidvania ability gates (the canonical "you cannot pass without X"), Zelda-style item gates, level gates in MMOs/open worlds. When are hard gates good (orientation, pacing) vs bad (softlock anxiety, checklist feel)? How do shipped games telegraph "you are not ready — come back with X" honestly?
2. SOFT GATES: stat/skill thresholds that change outcomes not access (F:NV skill checks, Disco Elysium white/red checks — red checks reopen once!), difficulty-rating displays that let the player knowingly overreach (Darkest Dungeon: you CAN send level-1 heroes into a level-3 dungeon — the price is stress/casualties; Battle Brothers contract skulls; Souls-games: everything is "attemptable"), resource-bypass gates (pay/solve differently: Outer Worlds "pay, kill, or hack" pattern; immersive sim "many ways in").
3. EQUIPMENT-AS-KEY precedents: quests requiring a rope/boat/torch — how games avoid making fetch-of-item feel like padding (BOTW durability-as-cost, survival crafting prep lists, TTRPG "expedition supply" systems e.g. Torchbearer, OSR encumbrance-as-prep).
4. TELEGRAPHING UNDEPREPARED RISK: how games communicate "attemptable but dangerous" — danger bands, skull ratings, scout reports, "recommended party" UI. What makes the warning credible vs ignorable?
5. FAILURE PATTERNS: gates that are really padding (collect-N-keys), soft gates that deceive (fake choice: "you can attempt" = mathematically impossible), requirements that punish experimentation, level-scaling that erases the meaning of requirements.

OUTPUT FORMAT

firstLines:
# Broadcast: broadcast-20261011-212006

**Prompt:** You are a senior game systems designer at a AAA studio, expert in RPG mechanics and progression/reward design. Do a thorough ONLINE RESEARCH (search the web, cite real sources — articles, GDC talks, papers, postmortems, dev blogs, TTRPG design essays) on the topic below, then synthesize findings.

CONTEXT
We are designing the quest system of a single-player idle/management RPG with D&D flavor. Quests are nodes in an OPPORTUNITY GRAPH; party members have stats and (planned) equippable skills/spells/items. We want rewards and capabilities that change what is POSSIBLE, not just what is likely.

DESIGN PROPOSAL UNDER EVALUATION (not yet decided): rewards come in 8 categories — ACCESS (unlock places/contacts/quests), INFORMATION (reveal requirements/dangers/approaches), MITIGATION (reduce damage/risk/consequences), EXCEPTION (ignore a rule in a compatible situation), CONVERSION (turn a resource/capability into a different advantage), SYNERGY (boost capabilities already owned), PERMANENT INVESTMENT (change a possibility/rule for future quests), CONSUMABLE/COUNTERMEASURE (one-shot answer to a specific threat). Skills/spells/items can likewise OPEN an approach, NEGATE a consequence, TRANSFORM a check into a compatible one, REVEAL hidden info, BYPASS a requirement, or MODIFY a mechanic's operation (e.g. alarm accumulates slower). Key constraint: avoid an explosion of hand-authored per-quest exceptions — effects should attach to declared surfaces (core variables, requirement types, effect categories), not to individual cases.

RESEARCH TOPIC — REWARDS THAT OPEN DOORS; CAPABILITIES THAT CHANGE RULES
How do shipped games and TTRPGs implement rewards and abilities that alter possibility space rather than power level?

Cover explicitly:
1. UNLOCK-TYPE rewards: metroidvania abilities-as-keys (double jump = access), XCOM strategy layer rewards (research/projects unlocking strategic options not stat +X%), roguelike meta-progression (new cards/relics/characters unlocked, not stat boosts), faction/contact unlocks (Fallen London qualities, Hades keepsakes/npcs, Sunless Skies officers). Why do unlock rewards feel richer than +X rewards, and what do designers say about "verbs vs numbers"?
2. RULE-CHANGING capabilities: exception-based design in TCGs (MtG "cards may break rules — card text beats rulebook"; Yu-Gi-Oh keyword soups), roguelike relics/items that rewrite mechanics (Slay the Spire relics: Snecko Eye, Frozen Egg; Isaac items), TTRPG moves/feats that create exceptions (Dungeon World moves, 13th Age icon relationships, GUMSHOE investigative abilities — auto-success on core clues!), perks that change systems not numbers (F:NV perks, Outer Worlds flaws).
3. INFORMATION-AS-REWARD: games where intel/maps/scouting is the loot (submarine/scouting mechanics, Metroid prime scan visor debates, XCOM intel resource, Battle Brothers contracts revealing difficulty, TTRPG clue economies — Gumshoe "spend pool for extra info"). When is info a satisfying reward vs a non-reward?
4. ARCHITECTURE for rule-changing effects without exception-hell: how engines implement declarative effect surfaces (modifier systems, event/hook architectures, tagging capabilities) — e.g. how MtG-like games categorize continuous/replacement/triggered effects; how RPG systems stack "conditional modifiers" (Pathfinder bonus types debates!). Any precedents for a SMALL taxonomy of effect categories staying manageably small?
5. FAILURE PATTERNS: unlock rewards that became chores (keys-as-padding), exception effects that broke balance forever (MtG power-creep cards, Pathfinder bonus stacking), information rewards players felt cheated by, permanent investments that trivialized later content.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- 4-8 PRINCIPLES, each as an actionable rule with source/evidence. Tag each: [validated by shipped game] / [design theory] / [community consensus] / [opinion].
- A comparison table: precedent → what the capability/reward changes → declared surface vs hand-authored exception → balance control.
- A short "If you only do 3 things" section — highest leverage for a small indie team.
- Dense bullets over prose. Flag where sources disagree.

# Broadcast: broadcast-20261011-212627

**Prompt:** You are a senior game systems designer at a AAA studio, expert in RPG mechanics, procedural generation and information design. Do a thorough ONLINE RESEARCH (search the web, cite real sources — articles, GDC talks, papers, postmortems, dev blogs, TTRPG design essays) on the topic below, then synthesize findings.

CONTEXT
We are designing the quest system of a single-player idle/management RPG with D&D flavor. Quests arrive as procedural OFFERS on a board (~8-10/month vs 4-5 feasible — scarcity is the point). An EXPLORER role already reveals information about quests (secondary stats, dangers, surveillance — a canon rule). Quests belong to families (stealth/combat/exploration/diplomacy/preparation).

DESIGN PROPOSAL UNDER EVALUATION (not yet decided): two linked ideas.
(a) STEERABLE GENERATION — the player can bias the offer generator toward preferred families/tags; the preference influences the distribution WITHOUT guaranteeing it (control without removing uncertainty or competing opportunities).
(b) TRANSVERSAL INTEL RESOURCE — a single limited currency tied to operational information/prep (knowing a mission better is a spendable advantage), instead of per-family currencies (stealth-coins, diplomacy-coins...). Open question: how to keep it scarce and meaningful without making resources too interchangeable.

RESEARCH TOPIC — PLAYER-STEERED GENERATION AND INTEL AS A RESOURCE
How do shipped games let players influence procedurally generated content streams, and how is information made into a spendable resource?

Cover explicitly:
1. STEERING precedents: Slay the Spire map — you SEE the node graph and choose the route (visibility = steering without guarantee); FTL sector choice; Battle Brothers contract board + settlement specializations (different towns offer different contracts — geography as steering); XCOM2 choosing which missions to respond to (interception decisions); Invisible Inc campaign map (choose which facility to raid → chosen reward type); Wildfrost/roguelike drafting (class tags weighting card pools); Monster Train path forks. What is the mechanism — route choice, tag weighting, reroll currency, board curation?
2. DRAFT/WEIGHTING systems: how card-battle/roguelike systems weight offers (tag-weighted reward pools, banish/reroll mechanics, "choose 1 of 3" curation, STS rare card pity systems); TTRPG random-tables-with-biases (weighted tables, advantage/disadvantage on tables). What keeps steering meaningful vs making generation effectively authored-by-player?
3. INTEL CURRENCIES: XCOM intel resource (spent on missions/crafting/dark-site reveals), recon/scouting spending (pre-mission intel in Shadow Tactics/Desperados? recon in XCOM LW), Sunless Sea favors/secrets, Fallen London item-economy, TTRPG "preparedness"/flashback spends (Blades flashback mechanic — retroactive prep as a spend!), GUMSHOE spend pools, Divinity OS2 persuasion-as-investment. Which intel economies stayed interesting vs became hoarded/ignored?
4. VISIBILITY LADDERS: partial-info structures (you know the family but not the twist; you see difficulty band but not exact odds — we already ship exact-odds preview once engaged), fog-of-war info design. How much should steering cost vs reveal?
5. FAILURE PATTERNS: steering that made generation bland (always-optimal filter), currencies that multiplied until meaningless, info players never bought, reroll systems that removed all uncertainty and broke the game.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- 4-8 PRINCIPLES, each as an actionable rule with source/evidence. Tag each: [validated by shipped game] / [design theory] / [community consensus] / [opinion].
- A comparison table: precedent → steering mechanism → what stays uncertain → cost of steering/intel.
- A short "If you only do 3 things" section — highest leverage for a small indie team.

# Broadcast: broadcast-20261011-212931

**Prompt:** You are a senior game systems designer at a AAA studio, expert in strategy/management games and time-pressure design. Do a thorough ONLINE RESEARCH (search the web, cite real sources — articles, GDC talks, papers, postmortems, dev blogs, TTRPG design essays) on the topic below, then synthesize findings.

CONTEXT
We are designing a single-player idle/management RPG. A village produces expeditions: multi-phase text quests (days-long, real-time accelerated). The player can't do everything: ~8-10 quest offers/month vs 4-5 feasible; a quest costs ~28 human-days of labor, wounds make members unavailable for X days, the expedition leader rules capacity (tired/wounded leader → no expeditions). Declined/expired quests have consequences but are not punishments.

DESIGN PROPOSAL UNDER EVALUATION (not yet decided): TIME = three distinct concepts — DURATION (how long an activity occupies), DEADLINE (by when it must be done), OPPORTUNITY WINDOW (an interval where an action is advantageous/possible without being a hard deadline). Quests COMPETE: preparing for one may mean abandoning another, delaying an investment, or losing a window. Village growth has 3 dimensions: VISIBILITY (how many opportunities you see/how much you know), CAPABILITY (which you can attempt — skills/prep), OPERATIONAL CAPACITY (how many in parallel — humans, leaders, buildings; possibly multiple parties). Growth must NOT make everything trivially easier — more expeditions also means more wear and management pressure.

RESEARCH TOPIC — TIME PRESSURE, OPPORTUNITY WINDOWS, AND PARALLEL CAPACITY
How do shipped strategy/management/idle games implement competing time pressures and bounded parallelism?

Cover explicitly:
1. DEADLINE precedents — the good and the infamous: XCOM2 mission timers (the controversy: hidden per-mission turn timers vs strategic Avatar countdown — community verdict on which pressure was fair), XCOM EU abduction missions (3 sites, choose 1, 2 panic — the canonical "competing opportunities" mechanic!), Battle Brothers contract deadlines + world crises (late-game war/invasion forcing prioritization), Frostpunk storm/arcs, Stardew/Sun Haven festival windows, Paradox ticking events. When does a deadline feel like strategy vs like harassment?
2. OPPORTUNITY WINDOWS (not deadlines): seasonal events, caravan schedules, "the pass is open while the snow holds" patterns, Rimworld incidents/opportunities, MMO timed events critiques. Distinction between "expires if ignored" vs "better if timed" — any shipped examples that do BOTH well?
3. PARALLEL CAPACITY: how games bound simultaneity — expedition/assignment slots (idle games: multiple parties out at once; Fallout Shelter dweller assignment; Assassin's Creed Odyssey mercenary board? AFK Journey/idle RPGs send-N-teams), roster-stamina/fatigue as the real limiter (Battle Brothers injuries+fatigue forcing B-teams, XCOM wounded soldiers forcing bench depth — THE precedent for operational capacity being a roster problem not a slot problem), leader/officer limits (Total War army-per-general cap, Crusader Kings council slots, Pokemon?). Where does "send multiple parties" break for small rosters?
4. GROWTH WITHOUT TRIVIALIZATION: escalation coupling (XCOM: as you grow, threats grow — panopticon pressure; Darkest Dungeon: roster churn is the balance; incremental games' prestige loops). What keeps more-parallel-quests from becoming pure acceleration?
5. FAILURE PATTERNS: timers added later that fans rejected (XCOM2 launch timers vs WotC fixes), busywork opportunity spam (notification fatigue, "chore map"), capacity limits that felt artificial ("why can't I send a second team?" complaints), parallel systems that made downtime dead time.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- 4-8 PRINCIPLES, each as an actionable rule with source/evidence. Tag each: [validated by shipped game] / [design theory] / [community consensus] / [opinion].
- A comparison table: precedent → time-pressure model → parallelism limiter → growth-pressure coupling.
- A short "If you only do 3 things" section — highest leverage for a small indie team.
- Dense bullets over prose. Flag where sources disagree.

Declined/expired quests have consequences but are not punishments.\n\nDESIGN PROPOSAL UNDER EVALUATION (not yet decided): TIME = three distinct concepts — DURATION (how long an activity occupies), DEADLINE (by when it must be done), OPPORTUNITY WINDOW (an interval where an action is advantageous/possible without being a hard deadline). Quests COMPETE: preparing for one may mean abandoning another, delaying an investment, or losing a window. Village growth has 3 dimensions: VISIBILITY (how many opportunities you see/how much you know), CAPABILITY (which you can attempt — skills/prep), OPERATIONAL CAPACITY (how many in parallel — humans, leaders, buildings; possibly multiple parties). Growth must NOT make everything trivially easier — more expeditions also means more wear and management pressure.\n\nRESEARCH TOPIC — TIME PRESSURE, OPPORTUNITY WINDOWS, AND PARALLEL CAPACITY\nHow do shipped strategy/management/idle games implement competing time pressures and bounded parallelism?\n\nCover explicitly:\n1. DEADLINE precedents — the good and the infamous: XCOM2 mission timers (the controversy: hidden per-mission turn timers vs strategic Avatar countdown — community verdict on which pressure was fair), XCOM EU abduction missions (3 sites, choose 1, 2 panic — the canonical \"competing opportunities\" mechanic!), Battle Brothers contract deadlines + world crises (late-game war/invasion forcing prioritization), Frostpunk storm/arcs, Stardew/Sun Haven festival windows, Paradox ticking events. When does a deadline feel like strategy vs like harassment?\n2. OPPORTUNITY WINDOWS (not deadlines): seasonal events, caravan schedules, \"the pass is open while the snow holds\" patterns, Rimworld incidents/opportunities, MMO timed events critiques. Distinction between \"expires if ignored\" vs \"better if timed\" — any shipped examples that do BOTH well?\n3. PARALLEL CAPACITY: how games bound simultaneity — expedition/assignment slots (idle games: multiple parties out at once; Fallout Shelter dweller assignment; Assassin's Creed Odyssey mercenary board? AFK Journey/idle RPGs send-N-teams), roster-stamina/fatigue as the real limiter (Battle Brothers injuries+fatigue forcing B-teams, XCOM wounded soldiers forcing bench depth — THE precedent for operational capacity being a roster problem not a slot problem), leader/officer limits (Total War army-per-general cap, Crusader Kings council slots, Pokemon?). Where does \"send multiple parties\" break for small rosters?\n4. GROWTH WITHOUT TRIVIALIZATION: escalation coupling (XCOM: as you grow, threats grow — panopticon pressure; Darkest Dungeon: roster churn is the balance; incremental games' prestige loops). What keeps more-parallel-quests from becoming pure acceleration?\n5. FAILURE PATTERNS: timers added later that fans rejected (XCOM2 launch timers vs WotC fixes), busywork opportunity spam (notification fatigue, \"chore map\"), capacity limits that felt artificial (\"why can't I send a second team?\" complaints), parallel systems that made downtime dead time.\n\nOUTPUT FORMAT\n- 4-8 PRINCIPLES, each as an actionable rule with source/evidence. Tag each: [validated by shipped game] / [design theory] / [community consensus] / [opinion].\n- A comparison table: precedent → time-pressure model → parallelism limiter → growth-pressure coupling.\n- A short \"If you only do 3 things\" section — highest leverage for a small indie team.\n- Dense bullets over prose. # Broadcast: broadcast-20261011-213146

**Prompt:** You are a senior game systems designer at a AAA studio, expert in prototyping methodology and simulation-driven design. Do a thorough ONLINE RESEARCH (search the web, cite real sources — articles, GDC talks, papers, postmortems, dev blogs, design methodology essays) on the topic below, then synthesize findings.

CONTEXT
We are designing a single-player idle/management RPG. We just finished a design layer ABOVE single quests: an OPPORTUNITY LAYER (quest families, requirement taxonomy, door-opening rewards, steerable offer generation, three kinds of time — duration/deadline/window — and village capacity in 3 dimensions: visibility/capability/operational-capacity). None of it is implemented yet; the single-quest engine exists (node-graph expeditions, skill checks, wound/death, Monte Carlo validation on authored scenario graphs).

DESIGN PROPOSAL UNDER EVALUATION (not yet decided): the first test of the meta-layer should be WITHOUT COMBAT — a minimal prototype validating the opportunity structure itself: (a) requirements correctly produce access/risk/efficiency differences; (b) multiple READABLE ways exist to satisfy the same requirement; (c) skills/rewards open genuinely different possibilities; (d) the explorer can be steered toward families; (e) quests generate future opportunities without a rigid sequence; (f) deadlines/concurrent activities produce real strategic decisions. Setup: 3 families × 3 difficulty tiers, existing stats, configurable requirements, FIXED configurable rewards (no direct stat increments — reward spirals out of scope for v0).

RESEARCH TOPIC — HOW TO PROTOTYPE A META-LAYER: METHODOLOGY
What are proven methods for validating a meta-game/economy/opportunity structure BEFORE building the full game?

Cover explicitly:
1. STRUCTURE-FIRST prototyping precedents: Soren Johnson / Cole Wehrle talks on prototyping the strategy layer; Sid Meier "one prototype" practices; how XCOM's strategy layer was paper-first (Jake Solomon talks?); spreadsheet/simulation-driven design (designing economy models in sheets before code — "machinations" framework by Joris Dormans, Machinations.io tool — formal economy diagrams you can simulate!). TTRPG solo-playtesting methods for meta-systems.
2. SIMULATION-BEFORE-UI: cases where Monte Carlo / agent-based sims validated meta-game structure (battle for balance — how auto-battler/idle devs validate pacing; AI-vs-AI self-play for board game balance — e.g. how Slay the Spire reportedly used metrics? what devs say about sim-driven balance); what CAN'T be validated in sim (fun, legibility) and needs humans.
3. READABILITY/LEGIBILITY testing of meta-systems: how to test "the player understands what opened what" — paper prototypes, Wizard-of-Oz text prototypes, single-page tabletop versions (digital game jam → boardgame conversions), tutorial-free comprehension tests. Any precedents from grand-strategy/4X tutorialization postmortems?
4. MINIMUM VIABLE META: how small can the first version be while still exposing real problems — "one loop" tests, fake-data harnesses, dev-console-driven playtests (play the system via commands, no UI). What metrics to pre-commit (decision distribution, dominant-strategy detection, dead-option rate, opportunity-miss rate)?
5. FAILURE PATTERNS: prototypes that validated nothing because scope crept; sims that produced false confidence (model != game); meta-layers that tested fine but collapsed on real UI; testing generation quality with too few samples.

OUTPUT FORMAT
- 4-8 PRINCIPLES, each as an actionable rule with source/evidence. Tag each: [validated by shipped game/method] / [design theory] / [community consensus] / [opinion].
- A comparison table: method → what it validates → what it can't validate → cost for a small team.
- A short "If you only do 3 things" section — highest leverage for a small indie team.
- Dense bullets over prose. Flag where sources disagree.

## Pattern 1 — «Il testimone non poteva vedere ciò che dichiarava» (3ª istanza di T-04) → PROPOSTA

### Signal
- Un claim di successo su animazione/sequenza/scena dopo una verifica fatta con strumenti che non possono osservare la cosa: browser pane `hidden` (viewport 0×0, rAF fermo), `getBoundingClientRect` di 3 immagini, `tsc` che si ferma agli errori di sintassi di un altro file (nessun controllo dei tipi, riportato comunque come «ok»).
- Un'anomalia osservata (marker che scivola 286→403 px) scritta come «da sapere» invece di indagata.
- Il criterio di accettazione è quello dell'autore («un solo goblin»), non quello del Director («l'evento giusto»).
